title: Paper 1 Question 2: Summary Skills
description: Selective summaries under exam conditions — reading for the focus, paraphrasing into your own words, staying inside 120 words, and answering the attitudes question.

notes.heading: The Task: Two Parts, Twenty Marks
notes.body: Paper 1 Question 2 is based on Text B and has two parts worth 20 marks in total. In 2(a) you write a selective summary: continuous writing of no more than 120 words, in your own words, covering only what the question's focus asks for. It carries 10 reading marks (R1 explicit meanings, R2 implicit meanings, R5 selecting information for a specific purpose) and 5 writing marks (W1–W3: expression, organisation, vocabulary and sentence variety). In 2(b) you answer a short-answer question about attitudes and opinions in the text, worth 5 marks (R2 and R3). Paper 1 lasts 2 hours for 80 marks, so Question 2 earns about 30 minutes of your time, including your share of the 15 minutes' reading time.

illustration.alt: A funnel diagram showing four narrowing stages of the Question 2(a) summary: read the whole text, select only focus-matching points, paraphrase them in your own words, and write continuous prose within the 120-word limit.
illustration.caption: A summary narrows the whole text to a 120-word answer: read everything, select only what the focus demands, paraphrase, then write it as linked prose.

notes.heading: Read for the Focus, Not the Whole Text
notes.body: Every 2(a) question names a focus — the one aspect of Text B your summary must cover, such as 'the difficulties the explorer faced' or 'the benefits of the new scheme'. Underline the focus words before you annotate anything. Then read Text B like a filter, not a net: mark only the material that serves the focus and mentally cross out the rest, however interesting it is. Content that does not match the focus earns nothing — this is R5, selecting and using information for a specific purpose, and it is what separates a selective summary from a general retelling. Apply one test to every candidate point: does this directly answer the question as worded? The close-reading craft underneath this is taught in Reading Comprehension and Text Analysis; here the exam pays you for aiming it.

notes.heading: One Point per Mark
notes.body: The 10 reading marks in 2(a) are content marks: broadly one mark per distinct, relevant point. That shapes the whole strategy — breadth beats depth. While annotating, look for MORE than ten candidate points, then select the ten strongest and clearest. A point is one complete idea: a fact, a reason, an effect. Saying the same thing twice in different words earns one mark, not two, so check your list for disguised repeats before drafting. Points can be explicit (stated directly) or implicit (clearly suggested), because R1 and R2 are both assessed. When you draft, give each point roughly one clause: ten points fit inside 120 words only if none of them sprawls into a sentence of its own.

notes.heading: Own Words: Paraphrase or Pay
notes.body: The task says 'in your own words', and the 5 writing marks are where copying is punished: W3 rewards a range of vocabulary that is yours, so lifted phrases earn nothing and mark the whole answer as derivative. Paraphrasing is a drillable skill. Swap synonyms ('gruelling' becomes 'punishing'), change the word form ('they were exhausted' becomes 'exhaustion set in'), flip the sentence structure ('the storm delayed them' becomes 'they were delayed by the storm'), or compress a specific image into a general statement. You may keep technical terms, numbers and proper nouns — 'Everest' has no synonym. A paraphrase must also keep the meaning: softening 'hostile' to 'unfriendly' loses the point. Build the skill by writing timed summaries against the course's free-response practice sets and reviewing the AI marking feedback.

notes.heading: Continuous Prose, No Trimmings
notes.body: Question 2(a) must be written as continuous prose — flowing, linked sentences. That means no bullet points, no numbered list, no headings. It also means no frame: do not open with 'This text is about...' or close with 'In conclusion...' — those words earn no content marks and eat your allowance. Use connectives to compress instead: 'although', 'because', 'while' and 'despite' let you join two points in one sentence, which is how ten points fit inside 120 words. One well-linked paragraph is enough; two short ones are fine. Finally, read your draft as a stranger would: a summary must stand alone, so if a sentence only makes sense to someone who has read Text B, rewrite it.

notes.heading: The 120-Word Ceiling
notes.body: 'No more than 120 words' is a hard ceiling, not a guideline: content written beyond the limit cannot help you, and the time it cost is gone. Aim to land between about 100 and 120 words — a 60-word answer has almost certainly missed content points, while a 165-word answer has burned time you owe the later questions. Practise counting until you can estimate by eye: learn how many words your handwriting fits per line, then count lines instead of words. Numbers and hyphenated words each count as one word. If a draft runs long, delete your weakest whole point rather than trimming every sentence into fragments — one dropped point costs one content mark, but mangled sentences cost writing marks too.

notes.heading: Question 2(b): Attitudes and Opinions
notes.body: Question 2(b) is a short-answer question about attitudes and opinions in Text B, worth 5 marks (R2 implicit meanings and attitudes, R3 analysing ideas with appropriate support). Attitude is how someone feels (angry, proud, resigned); opinion is what they think or believe (the scheme will fail). Both are usually implied rather than announced, so read the tone: verbs, adverbs and contrasts are the signals ('sighed', 'grudgingly', 'but'). Answer in clear statements, and support each one with a short quotation or close reference woven into your own sentence — 'the writer calls the promise "much-trumpeted", which suggests scepticism'. A quotation with no explanation shows you found the evidence but not that you understood it; always say what the words imply.

flashcards.definition: A summary that includes only the points matching the question's focus — not a retelling of the whole text.
flashcards.example: If the focus is 'difficulties at sea', the captain's childhood dreams stay out.

flashcards.definition: The specific aspect named in the question; it decides which points from the text earn marks.
flashcards.example: Underline it before annotating: 'Summarise the DIFFICULTIES the crew faced.'

flashcards.definition: Copying phrases straight from the text into your answer; it forfeits the own-words writing marks.
flashcards.example: Writing 'the journey was gruelling' word for word is lifting.

flashcards.definition: Restating an idea in your own words while keeping its meaning — the core skill of Question 2(a).
flashcards.example: 'The team was exhausted' becomes 'exhaustion set in'.

flashcards.definition: Connected prose sentences, as 2(a) requires — no bullet points, lists or headings.
flashcards.example: Use connectives like 'although' and 'because' to link points into sentences.

flashcards.definition: The 120-word maximum for 2(a); plan for 100–120 and learn to estimate by lines of handwriting.
flashcards.example: Numbers and hyphenated words each count as one word.

flashcards.definition: One distinct, relevant idea in a summary, worth broadly one reading mark; ten marks means about ten points.
flashcards.example: A fact, a reason, or an effect — each expressed once, in one clause.

flashcards.definition: Information stated directly in the text (R1) — the easiest points to harvest for a summary.
flashcards.example: 'The crossing took eleven days' is explicit.

flashcards.definition: Meaning suggested but not directly stated (R2); creditable in a summary if it matches the focus.
flashcards.example: 'She checked the map twice' implies she felt unsure of the route.

flashcards.definition: The feelings or stance a writer or speaker shows towards something — the target of Question 2(b).
Your own vocabulary and sentence structures; W3 rewards them, and copied phrases earn nothing.
flashcards.example: Keep technical terms and names ('Everest'); paraphrase everything else.

flashcards.definition: A short quote woven into your own sentence as evidence — ideal for supporting points about attitude.
flashcards.example: She calls the benefits 'much-trumpeted', showing doubt.

questions.stem: What does Paper 1 Question 2(a) ask you to produce?
choices: A retelling of everything that happens in Text B
A selective summary in your own words, covering only the question's focus
Your personal opinion of Text B
An analysis of the writer's language techniques
questions.explanation: 2(a) is a selective summary: the 10 reading marks (R1/R2/R5) reward only points matching the focus. A whole-text retell ignores selection; personal opinion belongs to other tasks; language analysis is Question 3's language task, not Question 2.

questions.stem: What is the maximum length of a Question 2(a) summary?
choices: 100 words
250 words
120 words
There is no limit
questions.explanation: The syllabus specifies continuous writing of no more than 120 words. 250 belongs to the Question 3 language task (200–250 words), 100 simply under-uses your allowance, and the limit is real — content beyond it cannot help you.

questions.stem: Question 2(a) carries 10 reading marks for content. What does that tariff imply a strong answer should contain?
choices: Around ten distinct, relevant points, each credited once
Two or three points developed at length
Ten direct quotations from Text B
One point for every paragraph of Text B
questions.explanation: One mark per content point means breadth wins: you need roughly ten separate ideas. Developing two points at length caps the content score near two marks; quotations are lifting, which the writing marks punish; and points do not map neatly to paragraphs — one paragraph may hold three points or none.

choices: Bullet points
A numbered list
A table of key points
Continuous writing in connected sentences
questions.explanation: The syllabus states the summary must be continuous writing. Bullets, numbering and tables all break that instruction and forfeit the organisation and expression credit (W2) that linked prose earns.

questions.stem: A question asks: 'Summarise the difficulties the crew faced at sea.' Text B also describes the captain's childhood dreams and the ship's unusual design. Which point belongs in the summary?
choices: The captain's childhood ambition to sail
The ship's innovative hull design
The storm that tore the mainsail and flooded the deck
The history of the harbour they departed from
questions.explanation: Only the storm is a difficulty the crew faced at sea — it answers the question as worded. Childhood dreams, hull design and harbour history are off-focus: interesting content earns nothing, and including it spends words from your 120.

questions.stem: Text B says: 'The journey was gruelling and the team was exhausted.' Which version keeps both ideas in your own words?
choices: The trip was punishing and left the group worn out.
The journey was gruelling and the team was exhausted.
The journey was difficult.
Gruelling journey; exhausted team.
questions.explanation: The first option swaps synonyms and restructures while keeping both ideas (the journey hard, the team exhausted). The second is pure lifting; the third drops the team point entirely; the fourth is note form, not the continuous prose the task requires.

questions.stem: A student opens their 2(a) answer: 'This fascinating text tells us a great deal about the expedition. The writer uses many techniques. Firstly,' What is wrong with this opening?
choices: Nothing — it politely sets the scene
It uses too many quotations
It should have been written in bullet points
It spends scarce words on an introduction that earns no content marks — a summary should start with the first credited point
questions.explanation: Every word that is not a relevant content point costs you, and 120 words leaves no room for a frame. There are no quotations here, and bullet points are banned; the fix is to delete the preamble and begin with point one.

questions.stem: Which of these may you keep from the text without penalty in a summary?
choices: Full sentences that express key ideas
Technical terms and proper nouns with no natural synonym
Any phrase of under ten words
The writer's most vivid metaphors
questions.explanation: Names and technical terms ('Everest', 'hypothermia') have no own-words equivalent, so keeping them is fine. Lifted sentences and long phrases are copying, and vivid metaphors are exactly the writer's words — the opposite of what W3 rewards.

questions.stem: For Question 2(b), which response best answers: 'What is the writer's attitude to the new development?'
choices: 'The writer quotes a councillor and a local resident.'
'The development is large and modern.'
'The writer is quietly sceptical — she calls the promised benefits 'much-trumpeted', suggesting she doubts them.'
'The text is an article about a development.'
questions.explanation: An attitude answer names a feeling or stance and supports it: 'quietly sceptical' plus the embedded quotation does both. Quoting sources identifies a feature, not an attitude; describing the development is about the topic; naming the genre says nothing about feeling.

questions.stem: A student's summary covers nine strong points but runs to 165 words. What is the best advice?
choices: Keep it — more words means more marks
Cut to 120 words; content beyond the limit cannot help you and the extra writing time is lost
Add a conclusion to balance the length
Switch to bullet points to save space
questions.explanation: The limit is a ceiling: trim by dropping the weakest whole point and tightening phrasing. Extra words add nothing creditable; a conclusion wastes still more words; and bullet points break the continuous-writing rule.

questions.stem: How many marks is Question 2(b) worth?
choices: 5 marks
10 marks
15 marks
20 marks
questions.explanation: 2(b) is the 5-mark short-answer question on attitudes and opinions (R2/R3). Ten is the reading tariff of 2(a), fifteen is all the reading marks across Question 2, and twenty is the whole of Question 2.

questions.stem: Which strategy best fits more credited content into the 120-word limit?
choices: Write longer sentences describing each point in detail
Add an evaluative comment after each point
Repeat the strongest point in fresh wording
Use connectives such as 'although' and 'because' to combine related points into one sentence
questions.explanation: Compound sentences with connectives carry two points for the price of one clause. Extra detail and evaluation are not content points, and a repeated point — however freshly worded — is credited only once.

questions.stem: Can an implicit point earn credit in a 2(a) summary?
choices: No — only directly stated facts count
Yes — R2 rewards understood implicit meanings, provided they match the focus and are in your own words
Yes, but only if you quote the exact phrase that implies it
Only in Question 2(b)
questions.explanation: The 2(a) reading marks include R2, implicit meanings, so a clearly implied idea is creditable. You still must not lift the phrasing — paraphrase is the rule — and inference is not confined to 2(b), which is a separate question about attitudes.

questions.stem: Text B includes: 'Another dawn, another double shift,' Mara sighed, though she admitted the extra pay would finally clear her debts. Which detail best supports the claim that Mara's attitude to the extra work is resigned but practical?
choices: 'Another dawn'
'clear her debts'
'sighed' combined with 'the extra pay would finally clear her debts' — weariness balanced against a benefit she accepts
'Mara'
questions.explanation: The mixed attitude lives in the combination: the sigh shows resignation, the pay shows the practical reason she accepts the work. Each half-quotation alone captures only one side of the attitude, and her name is not evidence of anything.

questions.stem: Paper 1 lasts 2 hours and carries 80 marks. About how long should you give Question 2 (20 marks), including your reading of Text B?
choices: About 30 minutes
About 10 minutes
About an hour
As long as it takes — timing does not matter
questions.explanation: The paper works out at roughly a minute and a half per mark, so 20 marks earns about 30 minutes. Ten minutes starves a quarter of the paper; an hour unbalances everything after it; and in a timed exam, pacing is a skill, not an option.
